ideas.title: Heart health finally gets a female definition: what the new AHA criteria for girls and women change, from puberty to menopause
ideas.angle: Heart disease is the top killer of women, yet the standard yardsticks were built on men. The piece asks what the new sex-specific criteria add (life stages like pregnancy and menopause) and whether doctors will actually use them, or whether it stays a guideline on paper.
ideas.why_now: Joint guidance led by the AHA was just issued and lands in the same week as the NIH women's health division and task force news.
ideas.is_it_real: The guidance itself is solid: it is an official AHA newsroom release from leading professional groups. It is clinical guidance, not a new study, so frame it that way. Specific contents must come from the published statement, not the press release alone (upstream check flagged minor issues).
terms: aha leading health groups redefine heart health criteria for girls and women

ideas.title: KFF's fall poll: who Americans trust on vaccines now
ideas.angle: One sharp stat from KFF's fall trust tracker, with a one-line take on what it means heading into flu and measles season. It pairs naturally with the measles/SSPE pitch already in motion.
ideas.why_now: KFF released its Fall 2026 update on vaccine views this week.
ideas.is_it_real: KFF is a reliable pollster, but this is self-reported opinion data. Present it as a trust metric and pull the actual numbers from the KFF report; none are in hand yet.

ideas.title: A PTSD treatment with a '68% remission' rate: what that number does and doesn't mean
ideas.angle: A short, skeptical item on a headline remission rate: what the treatment is, how big and long the trial was, and what remission means in trial terms.
ideas.why_now: Trial results were publicized Oct. 22 and the 68% figure is the kind of number that travels.
ideas.is_it_real: So far this rests on a single ScienceDaily summary. The trial phase, sample size, comparator and journal are unconfirmed. It only runs if the writer can find the paper, and it should not be upgraded to a pitch on this evidence.

ideas.title: Is it real? The 'non-toxic air fryer': PFAS fear, ceramic marketing, and what the coatings actually do
ideas.angle: Searches for a 'non-toxic' air fryer keep climbing. The post checks whether nonstick coatings in air fryers pose a real exposure risk at normal temperatures, or whether 'non-toxic' is mostly a marketing label for ceramic and stainless models. It ties into her own kitchen gut-reno choices.
ideas.why_now: The term has been rising on and off for about a month and is still climbing, which suits an evergreen 'is it real?' post. It is a candidate for next Wednesday, since this week's slot already went to the AI diagnosis post.
ideas.is_it_real: The search trend is real and sustained. The underlying claim is checkable against published research on PTFE/PFAS and FDA food-contact rules, but no sources are in hand yet and none are cited here. The post needs its own receipts.

notes: The wide trending feed was almost all sports, celebrities and politics. The keepers came from the newsroom pipeline: two attach to yesterday's ideas (the NIH task force and the cheese recall), and the AHA women's heart-health guidance is the one fresh pitch. Women's health is clustering this week (NIH division, task force, AHA criteria), which could support a bigger 'women's health moment' piece if editors bite on the pitches. Humana, Risant Health and Abbott Nutrition appeared with no context; they are on watch because open enrollment or a formula issue could turn any of them into a story. TFM already has this Wednesday's post, so the air fryer idea is queued for the following week.
